precepts.text: Dreams lift up fools; whoso regardeth dreams is like him that catcheth at a shadow. Don't chase dreams. But verse 3 gives you a clue to understanding dreams from God: the vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the likeness of a face to a face. You could dream about somebody you know, but it's not them; it's someone similar, in age or in what they do. You just have to know the people in your circle.
precepts.point: Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.
precepts.why:
The butler and the baker of the king of Egypt offended their lord and were put in ward “the place where Joseph was bound.” “they dreamed a dream both of them, each man his dream in one night,” and in the morning they were sad, because “there is no interpreter of it.” Joseph answered, “Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you.”

Sirach speaks to dreams: “The hopes of a man void of understanding are vain and false: and dreams lift up fools.” “Whoso regardeth dreams is like him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind.” Don't chase dreams; a man who lives by every dream is grasping at shadows.

But verse 3 gives a clue to understanding the dreams that come from God: “The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the likeness of a face to a face.” You may dream about somebody you know, say a man named Joe, and see Joe's face; but it is not Joe. It is someone similar to Joe, maybe in age or in what they do for a living. It could be Bob. You just have to know the people in your circle.

That is how the dreams in Genesis 40 work. The butler's vine with “three branches” and the baker's “three white baskets” were resemblances of one thing to another: the three branches and the three baskets were three days. The interpretation belonged to God, and Joseph gave it.

precepts.text: They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me: meaning he would never get out. It's talking about Israel in captivity, which goes with political prisoners who have been in there a long time.
precepts.point: Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.
precepts.why:
After interpreting the butler's dream, Joseph asked him, “think on me when it shall be well with thee,” and “make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house:” “For indeed I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews: and here also have I done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.” He wanted out of that dungeon.

Notice the prison is called a dungeon. Lamentations uses the same word: “They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me.” To cast a stone upon him means he would never get out. It is speaking of Israel in captivity.

That goes with our political prisoners, who have been in there for a long time, cut off in the dungeon with a stone cast over them. Joseph, stolen away and imprisoned though he had done nothing, is a picture of his people in captivity.

precepts.text: Let the day perish wherein I was born. This is how the Hebrews felt regarding birthdays.
precepts.point: Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.
precepts.why:
Joseph's interpretations came to pass “the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, that he made a feast unto all his servants.” On that birthday “he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again,” “But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them.”

Wherever you read of a birthday in scripture, Pharaoh's birthday, Herod's birthday, the birthday of one of the Greek kings, something bad happens. Here a man is hanged at a birthday feast. A birthday is a day of narcissism, a day of proclaiming yourself to be God.

Job shows how the Hebrews felt about the day of their birth: “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived.” A righteous man did not exalt the day he was born; he wished it would perish. That is why we never celebrated birthdays.

precepts.text: Cursed be the day wherein I was born. Jeremiah is saying the same thing Job said. We never celebrated birthdays; that custom came from the nations, from what they dug up in their archaeological digs. It is not of God.
precepts.point: Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.
precepts.why:
Jeremiah says the same thing Job said: “Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed.” Two prophets, and neither one blessed the day of his birth. Put that together with Pharaoh's birthday in Genesis 40, where the baker was hanged at the feast.

We never celebrated birthdays. They are days of narcissism, days to put ourselves up above God. The custom came from the nations; it came through the white man, who got it from what they dug up in their archaeological digs, and then taught that we should be celebrating birthdays.

So stop celebrating that foolishness, even with the excuse that it's for the children. Shut up, you narcissist. It is not of God. It's of the devil. And after that birthday feast, “Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.”

precepts.text: Your God is a God of gods and a revealer of secrets; the same God that gave Joseph interpretations gave them to Daniel.
precepts.point: Daniel stood in the same understanding in Babylon; the king confessed that Daniel's God is a God of gods and a revealer of secrets. Joseph already understood that these things belong to the Most High.

note.label: Genesis 40: Do Not Interpretations Belong to God

precepts.why:
“The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret.” Daniel stood in Babylon in the same understanding Joseph had in the prison, and even the king of Babylon had to confess it: Daniel’s God is a God of gods and a revealer of secrets.

The butler and the baker said, “We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it.” Joseph answered on another level: “Do not interpretations belong to God?” They do. The same God that gave Joseph the interpretations gave them to Daniel. Joseph already understood that these things belong to the Most High, and that is why he could say, tell me them.

precepts.text: The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another; the threes in both dreams stood for three days.
precepts.point: Both men saw variations of three, and in both dreams the three stood for three days. The dream is not always what is seen: the vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the likeness of a face to a face. You may see yourself steal a piece of bread in a dream, and the meaning is that somebody will steal something from you in the days ahead; one thing resembles another.

note.label: Genesis 40: Do Not Interpretations Belong to God

precepts.why:
“The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the likeness of a face to a face.” A dream is not always what is seen; one thing resembles another. You may see yourself steal a piece of bread in a dream, and the meaning is that somebody will steal something from you in the days ahead.

So the chief baker’s “three white baskets” were not baskets: “The three baskets are three days.” The butler saw a variation of three and the baker saw a variation of three, and in both dreams the three stood for three days. The likeness was the same, but the ends were not: within three days Pharaoh would “lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee.”

precepts.text: On Herod's birthday the dancing pleased him, and the head of John the Baptist was demanded in a charger; another wicked occurrence on a birthday.
precepts.point: Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.

note.label: Genesis 40: Do Not Interpretations Belong to God

precepts.why:
“But when Herod’s birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod.” He promised with an oath to give her whatsoever she would ask, and she, instructed of her mother, said, “Give me here John Baptist’s head in a charger.” John the Baptist was beheaded on a birthday.

Birthdays are heathen customs, and wicked things take place at them. On Pharaoh’s birthday he made a feast unto all his servants and “hanged the chief baker”, a man put to death before everybody. On Herod’s birthday the dancing pleased him and the head of John the Baptist was demanded in a charger. Two birthdays in the scriptures, and a man dies at each one.
